title: Microservice Communication Patterns: Quick Revision
summary: Night-before revision notes on how services talk: sync REST/gRPC versus async messaging, API gateway, service discovery, load balancing, idempotency, and event-driven architecture with pub/sub.

chapters.title: Sync vs Async Mental Model
points: Sync request/response: caller blocks until the callee replies, so the two are coupled in time and availability
Async messaging: caller publishes to a broker and moves on; the consumer processes later, so the two are decoupled in time
Availability math: a sync chain of N services at 99.9% each gives about 99.9%^N overall, while a broker absorbs downstream outages
Pick sync when the caller needs the answer now (reads, auth checks); pick async for work that can finish later (emails, billing, fan-out)
Common mistake: chaining sync calls across many services creates cascading failures and latency that adds up; fix it with timeouts, circuit breakers or async events

chapters.title: REST vs gRPC vs Message Broker
points: REST: HTTP/1.1 plus JSON, resource URLs and verbs (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE); human readable, cache friendly, best for public APIs
gRPC: HTTP/2 plus Protobuf with a .proto contract; binary, smaller, supports multiplexing and streaming (unary, server, client, bidirectional)
Comparison: REST for browsers and public clients, gRPC for internal low-latency service-to-service calls, broker for fire-and-forget or fan-out

Broker delivery semantics: at-most-once may lose messages, at-least-once may duplicate them (the usual default), exactly-once is costly and effectively achieved by at-least-once plus idempotent consumers
Common mistake: exposing gRPC directly to browsers (needs gRPC-Web or a gateway), or changing Protobuf field numbers (never reuse or renumber them, only add new fields)

chapters.title: API Gateway, Service Discovery and Load Balancing
points: API gateway: single entry point for clients that handles routing, authentication, rate limiting, TLS termination, request aggregation and protocol translation
Service discovery: services register with a registry (Consul, Eureka, etcd, Kubernetes DNS) and heartbeats remove dead instances, so no hardcoded IPs
Client-side discovery (client queries the registry and picks an instance, e.g. Eureka) versus server-side (client calls a load balancer or DNS name, e.g. Kubernetes Service)
Load balancing algorithms: round robin, weighted round robin, least connections, IP hash or consistent hash for sticky routing; L4 balances on TCP, L7 on HTTP path and headers
Common mistake: a gateway turned into a business-logic monolith or a single point of failure (run it replicated), and health checks that only test the port instead of real readiness

chapters.title: Idempotency and Safe Retries
points: Idempotent operation: repeating it N times gives the same end state as doing it once; GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent, POST is not by default
Idempotency key: client sends a unique key (Idempotency-Key header); server stores key plus response and returns the stored result on a repeat instead of reprocessing
Implementation: insert the key with a unique constraint in the same transaction as the side effect, so concurrent duplicates fail instead of both running
Consumers must dedupe by message ID or use naturally idempotent writes (upsert, SET status='paid') because brokers deliver at-least-once
Common mistake: retrying non-idempotent calls like payments without a key, retrying without exponential backoff plus jitter, or keeping keys forever instead of with a TTL

chapters.title: Event-Driven Architecture and Pub/Sub
points: Event: an immutable fact that already happened (OrderPlaced), named in past tense; a command is a request to do something (PlaceOrder) with one intended receiver
Pub/sub: publishers send to a topic and every subscribed consumer group gets a copy; a queue instead delivers each message to exactly one competing consumer
Kafka-style log: topics split into partitions, ordering is guaranteed only within a partition (pick the key, such as orderId), and consumer groups track offsets and can replay
Reliability patterns: transactional outbox (write event and data in one DB transaction, then relay), dead-letter queue for poison messages, saga for distributed transactions

Common mistake: assuming global ordering, skipping the outbox so the DB write and publish diverge (dual write), no DLQ so one bad message blocks the stream, and breaking event schemas without versioning

chapters.title: Communication Patterns Cheat Sheet
points: Decision table: need the answer now means REST or gRPC; can finish later or fan out means broker; public clients mean REST via gateway; internal hot path means gRPC
Resilience defaults: set timeouts, retry with exponential backoff plus jitter, add circuit breakers, and cap retries so they do not storm a struggling service
Delivery rule: at-least-once delivery plus idempotent consumers equals effectively exactly-once
Queue versus topic: queue means one consumer gets each message; pub/sub topic means every subscriber group gets a copy; Kafka orders per partition only
Infrastructure recap: gateway for edge concerns, registry or DNS for discovery, L4 or L7 load balancer for distribution, outbox plus DLQ plus saga for reliable events
